title: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma with APC and EGFR L858R co-mutations: a case report
author: Vitor Jodar Cavalheiro; Daniel Santos Rocha Sobral Filho; Giulia Mazaro de Oliveira; Manuela del Rio Navarrete da Fonseca; Gabriel Travessini; Ibere Cauduro Soares; Gilberto de Castro Junior; Jorge Sabbaga; Milena Perez Mak; Paulo Marcelo Gehm Hoff
text:
Abstract
Mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene are frequent in colorectal cancer (CRC), whereas epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations, particularly the L858R variant, are exceedingly rare. Their coexistence in CRC is rare and poorly described in the literature and poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. We describe a 69-year-old man with a history of resected CRC who presented with a lung mass and adrenal lesions, initially suspected as metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Biopsy revealed poorly differentiated carcinoma with immunohistochemistry suggestive of gastrointestinal origin. Due to doubts regarding the primary site, it was decided to start systemic treatment with mFOLFIRINOX while awaiting NGS. After 7 cycles, a partial radiologic and clinical response was observed. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) became available and identified an EGFR L858R mutation, favoring NSCLC. Chemotherapy was paused, and the patient was treated with gefitinib. Rapid disease progression ensued, with new brain metastases. Expanded NGS subsequently revealed concurrent APC and TP53 pathogenic variants, confirming the diagnosis of metastatic CRC harboring co-occurring EGFR and APC mutations. The patient died 10 months after diagnosis. This case underscores the critical role of comprehensive molecular profiling via NGS in accurately diagnosing complex oncologic presentations. To our knowledge, this is the first case report of APC and EGFR L858R co-mutation in colorectal cancer. For this patient, the misclassification delayed the use of more appropriate therapies for CRC, which may have impacted clinical outcomes.
Keywords: colorectal cancer, EGFR L858R mutation, APC mutation, next-generation sequencing
Key Points.
The coexistence of APC and EGFR L858R mutations in colorectal cancer is extremely rare and has not been previously reported.
This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing metastatic colorectal cancer from primary lung cancer when relying on limited molecular data.
Comprehensive next-generation sequencing is essential to avoid misclassification and to guide appropriate therapy in complex oncologic presentations.
Introduction
Mutations in the tumor suppressor gene Adenomatous Polyposis Coli (APC) are found in 80% of sporadic colorectal cancer (CRC) cases and are well-established in the development of the inherited form of CRC—Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP). APC mutations play a central role in tumorigenesis initiation by disrupting Wnt/β-catenin signaling and are often early events in CRC development.1,2
EGFR mutations are less common in CRC compared to non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). While approximately 60% of CRC cases exhibit aberrant EGFR signaling, primarily through overexpression, gene amplification (1%) and EGFR mutations (2%-3%) remain rare.3,4 Most EGFR mutations in CRC are found in exon 18, differing from NSCLC, where mutations typically occur in exons 19 and 21. Among identified oncogenic variants, the L858R mutation (exon 21) has been described but is extremely rare, representing less than 1%.3 When present, such mutations may act as drivers of tumor progression, aiding in distinguishing the primary tumor site in cases with ambiguous clinical and radiographic presentations.5,6
Emerging evidence highlights challenges in treating CRC cases with EGFR mutations. While EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) serve as first-line therapy in advanced EGFR-mutated NSCLC, their efficacy in EGFR-mutant CRC is limited due to intrinsic resistance mechanisms, often mediated by co-mutations in other signaling pathways, including APC. This underscores the necessity of a tailored therapeutic approach that integrates both the molecular landscape and tumor histopathology to optimize treatment outcomes.7,8
The co-occurrence of APC and EGFR mutations has been scarcely reported, and its clinical implications remain underexplored. The use of next-generation sequencing (NGS) has been instrumental in uncovering these rare molecular profiles, enabling more precise tumor characterization.9
Here, we present a unique case of a patient with a previous history of CRC, initially suspected of having a new primary NSCLC due to the presence of the EGFR L858R mutation in a lung biopsy. The patient received gefitinib but experienced significant disease progression, ultimately leading to death. Subsequent NGS revealed the presence of an APC mutation, indicating that the case was actually metastatic colorectal cancer with EGFR/APC co-mutations.
Patient story
The patient was a 69-year-old male, a former smoker (8 pack-years) until 1993, with a history of localized colorectal adenocarcinoma treated with surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy in 2015. There is no available information regarding the adjuvant treatment administered, as the patient was unable to report the treatment details and the medical records were not accessible. He was discharged from oncology follow-up in 2020 due to the absence of recurrence.
In 2023, the patient presented with a dry cough, right hemithorax pain, and weight loss. He was referred to our oncology center with suspected metastatic lung cancer.
A CT scan (Figure 1A) revealed a neoplastic lesion in the left lower lung lobe, measuring 13.0 × 9.6 × 10.6 cm, with mediastinal lymph node enlargement. The adrenal glands were also enlarged (right: 9.1 cm; left: 7.7 cm) (Figure 1C), with suspicious hepatic nodules. A head CT showed no suspicious lesions. Colonoscopy findings were unremarkable.
Bronchoscopy revealed an obstructive vegetative lesion in the posterior segmental bronchus of the left lower lobe. Biopsy showed poorly differentiated carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was positive for AE1/AE3, CK20, and CDX-2 and negative for CK7, chromogranin A, TTF-1, and p63, suggesting either a primary NSCLC with intestinal differentiation or a gastrointestinal primary site.
Due to the inconclusive pathology findings, a multidisciplinary discussion was conducted. Imaging findings favored advanced NSCLC with adrenal involvement, while immunohistochemistry suggested a gastrointestinal origin. Considering the patient’s history, first-line systemic treatment with mFOLFIRINOX (infusional 5-FU, leucovorin, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin) was initiated, as it is active in both lung and colorectal cancer, while awaiting NGS results. Although a standard option would have been FOLFOX plus bevacizumab, this was not feasible due to the unavailability of bevacizumab in the Brazilian public health system. Therefore, mFOLFIRINOX was selected to offer a higher expected response rate compared to FOLFOX alone.
After seven chemotherapy cycles (November 14, 2023–March 11, 2024), partial response was observed (Figure 1B and D) per RECIST v1.1,10 with marked respiratory symptom improvement.
Molecular tumor board
NGS was performed using a customized panel of 40 genes with SureSelect (Agilent) for library preparation chemistry on the Illumina MiSeq platform, with data analyzed using SureCall v.4.2 (Agilent) and the GRCh37 reference genome.
NGS results, available in March 2024 (after seven cycles of chemotherapy), identified an EGFR c.2573T>G p.(L858R) mutation in exon 21 with a variant allele frequency (VAF) of 5.2%. Given the imaging findings and the driver EGFR mutation, NSCLC was favored. Chemotherapy was paused, and an oral EGFR-TKI (gefitinib) was initiated two weeks after the seventh cycle.
Following gefitinib initiation, the patient experienced progressive respiratory worsening, with dyspnea and cough. One month later, he was admitted to the emergency department with significant dyspnea. New CT scans (Figure 2A and B) showed progressive lung disease with bronchial obstruction and new central nervous system lesions (Figure 3A and B). Cranial CT, rather than MRI, was performed due to greater accessibility and faster availability within the Brazilian public healthcare system.
At this stage, an expanded NGS panel was requested, revealing pathogenic variants in APC (c.1495C>T p.(R499*)) and TP53 (c.438G>A p.(W146*)), with VAF of 44.2% and 46.8%, respectively. These findings clarified the diagnosis as metastatic CRC with EGFR/APC co-mutation.
Patient update
On June 17, 2024, the patient underwent conformal (3D) radiotherapy to the left pulmonary hilum (800 cGy, single fraction) to relieve dyspnea. Despite symptom relief, his condition continued to decline, leading to palliative care initiation. He remained hospitalized for symptom control and died on August 04, 2024, 10 months after the metastatic adenocarcinoma diagnosis.
Discussion
This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing between a new primary malignancy and metastatic disease in patients with prior cancer. Following systemic treatment with a regimen active in both lung and colorectal cancer, a clinical and radiological response was observed. The initial detection of the EGFR L858R mutation in lung lesions suggested primary lung adenocarcinoma, leading to gefitinib administration—a standard first-line therapy in NSCLC harboring EGFR mutations.11 Osimertinib is not available in the Brazilian public healthcare system. Therefore, gefitinib was used as the accessible EGFR inhibitor.
However, the lack of response and disease progression within three months raised doubts about the diagnosis, as gefitinib typically achieves a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 10.8 months in NSCLC.12 Expanded NGS identified an APC mutation, confirming the diagnosis as metastatic CRC rather than de novo NSCLC, explaining gefitinib’s inefficacy.
Although case reports have described responses to osimertinib in colorectal cancer with EGFR mutations, these findings remain limited to individual cases and have not been incorporated into major clinical guidelines.13,14 The intention was to reintroduce systemic chemotherapy. However, due to subsequent complications, the patient was unable to receive treatment for colorectal cancer and died.
APC mutations are characteristic of colorectal tumors. The co-occurrence of APC and EGFR mutations is rare and poorly documented but may define a unique molecular subset of colorectal cancer, potentially influencing tumor biology.2 Additionally, the presence of the TP53 co-occurring mutation, as observed here, is common in CRC and may indicate a more aggressive tumor phenotype, potentially responsive to therapies like cetuximab.15 Further studies are needed to explore this association.
In metastatic CRC, the role of EGFR mutations—particularly L858R—is not well-defined. While EGFR overexpression is linked to tumor differentiation and prognosis, activating mutations like L858R are exceedingly rare.16 No cases of colorectal cancer harboring APC mutations co-occurring with EGFR L858R have been reported in cBioPortal.17
This case underscores the critical role of comprehensive molecular profiling via NGS in complex oncologic diagnosis. Misinterpretation of a single mutation can lead to therapeutic errors, delaying appropriate treatment.18 To our knowledge, this is the first report of CRC harboring co-occurring APC and EGFR L858R mutations. Expanding NGS use in ambiguous cases not only aids diagnosis but also enhances understanding of rare molecular alterations and their clinical significance.
